doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Building the jazz program, tenure and Krivin's vision
summary: The first jazz bachelor's degree in the area, university leeway for working artists, family finances, and Northwestern contrast.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: program became really visible, he made it such that if another university was going to hire a jazz musician who had notoriety, they had to let them continue to be who they were, because that’s why they wanted them. So I would tell people, I said, “Well listen, if they want you to be who you are, then they’re going to have to give you some leeway to go out to travel to continue to do what you do.” Now there is a price for everything. So I mean I had to kind of, I couldn’t fly off just — because I was being paid, and it brought some stability into my home to the point where we were able to save enough money to send our son to the university without completely having to — my son went to Carnegie Mellon so I told him I had to charge more for quarter notes, as a bass player. But the thing was, it’s an expensive school. But he chose it. I said, “Okay, you’re going to have to do real well.” And he did. And he’s working. But the university did help us. And then I began to research — I mean the classical department musicians have been doing it for years. I mean concert pianists, cellists, violinists — they travel all over the world and they’re the residents at Juilliard, or they’re at Northwestern, or whatever. But all of a sudden it became a problem for a jazz musician to have to significant program at a university and still be able to do what he or she does. And I think Marty Krivin was helpful with me, and adamant about it, that other universities had to — a lot of people wanted — you have to have a doctorate in this. And there were no doctors in music. And Billy Taylor was probably it for the thirty years before anybody was a doctorate in music. But the life studies I had published, I was on a lot of recordings which were called publishing but I actually had a textbook and I had all of these things. So he actually put my portfolio so well together that it was almost a no-brainer for the school to go for it. Now I guess I was on probation, I guess this is where you have tenure and all that kind of stuff, and he helped me do all that. Because I didn’t know anything about it, I didn’t care less about it. I even said if some of the faculty people are really going to be kind of funky to me or not being continualized to it, because well I’m out of here. I don’t need it. And so I had some great allies. And before I left, one of the best recitals was a pianist and his recital he played solo piano, he played arias and he played trios, and then he took intermission and he came back and played some jazz, and then he wrote a big band chart, and it was like, and I said that’s possible. He wasn’t a great jazz musician but he had a breadth. He’s working now. He’s always going to work. I said that’s what can happen. I went to Northwestern University, you know, and they didn’t talk about film scoring. They didn’t talk about any of these other things that actually, at that time, when I went to school there, it was electronic music but it was really like really out kind of stuff at that time. I mean avante garde or very not tonal stuff. And jazz was, what? But that’s a different day now. And so I know what can — and Marty had the vision. And he taught me that it can happen.
